solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Composer and tot meeting woman outside church

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so one part wraps around another

parts.note: to tot up is to add, and a tot is a sum
a woman's name
standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A composer and a toddler meet a woman just outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' joins the two outer pieces, which then sit outside the church abbreviation: S(CH)UMANN.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Schumann was a German Romantic composer of piano music, songs and symphonies.

clue.text: Keep mum enthusiastic about religion

parts.note: the sound used to tell someone to keep quiet
to be into something is to be keen on it

explanation.surface: Someone is told to stay quiet about their passion for faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother but means silent, as in 'mum's the word'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shinto is the indigenous faith of Japan, centred on worship of kami spirits at shrines.

clue.text: Gardeners keeping quiet as optimistic folk?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one part holds another within

parts.note: people who use a hoe on the soil
p is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: Gardeners working silently are cheerful types.
explanation.walkthrough: The gardeners are defined by their tool, a hoe, and they hold the musical quiet sign: HO(P)ERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who hopes for good outcomes is an optimist; the word is a plain agent noun from the verb.

clue.text: Fancy a lady going after fellow in foreign city!

parts.note: a fellow is a man

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or decorated, so the letters are worked into a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An exclamation at the sight of a woman chasing a man around abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as the exclamation of surprise, but it is the rearrangement signal. 'Going after' puts the rearranged pair after the fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Mandalay is a major city in Myanmar, the old royal capital of Burma, famous from Kipling's poem.

clue.text: Upsetting shock makes one crazy

indicators.note: to upset is literally to tip over, and in a down clue that flips the order top to bottom

parts.note: to shock someone is to stun them

explanation.surface: A distressing shock can send a person mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upsetting' sounds emotional but in a down clue it means turning upside down, so the word reads from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is informal slang for mad or insane, used as a predicate adjective.

clue.text: Sailor is positioned the wrong way round in descent

definitions.note: noun in the clue, the answer is usually a verb or noun for the rope descent

parts.note: AB is able seaman, a sailor

indicators.note: facing the opposite direction means the letters run back to front

parts.note: something positioned somewhere lies there

explanation.surface: A sailor ends up upside down while climbing down.
explanation.walkthrough: AB for able-bodied seaman is a standard crossword sailor; only the second piece is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: An abseil is a controlled descent of a cliff or wall using a rope fixed above.

clue.text: Lout turning up, unable to say much and stroppy

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning upward means reading from the bottom to the top

parts.note: a lob is an old word for a clumsy lout or bumpkin
a shy person says little

explanation.surface: A yob arrives, tongue-tied and in a foul mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' looks like arriving, but in a down clue it means the word is written bottom to top. Stroppy and bolshy are British informal words for awkward and rebellious.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for uncooperative and bad-tempered, bolshy coming from Bolshevik.

clue.text: Old joke good editor crossed out

parts.note: ex means former
a pun is a joke on words
standard abbreviation for good
standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A stale joke is struck from the copy by a sensible editor.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word is a straight piece in order; the last two words are the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To expunge is to erase or strike out, so something expunged has been deleted from a text.

clue.text: Discard amateur leading a team

indicators.note: going in front means placing one part before the next one

parts.note: lay means non-professional, as in a layman
a side is a sports team

explanation.surface: An unpaid enthusiast captaining a squad is dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' suggests captaining, but it only places the first piece in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay something aside is to put it away or abandon it, a phrasal synonym for getting rid of.

clue.text: Mischief-maker, one to get freedom from punishment

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous sprite
unity is the number one

explanation.surface: A troublemaker gets away with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' usually gives I or A, but here it is the full word for the quantity one.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with impunity means acting without fear of penalty or consequences, an exact dictionary sense.

clue.text: Careless agent has left work to be collected

indicators.note: things collected are gathered up and held inside something else

parts.note: a secret agent is a spy
standard abbreviation for left
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A negligent agent has abandoned paperwork for someone else to pick up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb meaning abandoned, but it is the abbreviation L; with the work, it goes inside the agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloppy describes slapdash or untidy work, the same as being careless.

clue.text: Having different bands of inconsistent quality

definitions.meaning: first meaning: marked with stripes of varying colour
second meaning: uneven, good in patches

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bands' suggests music groups, but it means stripes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes both striped bacon or paint and a sports performer whose form comes and goes.

clue.text: Something that may leave black stain on brown cloth

parts.words: Something that may leave black stain
parts.note: tar is black and sticky and marks what it touches
tan is a light brown colour

explanation.surface: A warning about something leaving dark marks on a brown fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: The long opening phrase is a descriptive clue for one short word, then a colour follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tartan is the woollen fabric woven in a checked pattern, associated with Scottish clans.

clue.text: Pieces of artwork at a higher level that one is invited to see?

definitions.text: Pieces of artwork at a higher level that one is invited to see?

parts.words: Pieces of artwork at a higher level
parts.note: surface reading: prints hanging upstairs in someone's home
setter's reading: the old seducer's line, 'come up and see my ...'

explanation.walkthrough: The clue alludes to the cliché chat-up invitation to come upstairs to see one's artworks, a pretext for seduction.
explanation.definitionFit: These are prints made from acid-bitten metal plates, the artworks of the famous pickup line.

clue.text: First person, having pierced a fish, is sorry

definitions.note: the clue phrase is verb plus adjective; the answer is the adjective

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: piercing means pushing into, so one part goes inside another

parts.note: the shad is a herring-like fish
the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: Someone who has speared a fish feels guilty about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' suggests I, but the object pronoun is needed here, placed inside the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ashamed means feeling guilt or remorse, which is what being sorry is.

clue.text: See funny fellow stagger around

indicators.note: spinning around jumbles the order of the letters

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Watch the comedian lurch about the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stagger' looks like the verb describing the comic, but its seven letters are the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A gagster is a comedian or joker who tells gags, so a humorous man.

clue.text: Article stuck in piece of furniture may be necklace component

indicators.note: something stuck in is lodged inside, so one part sits within another

parts.note: a bed is furniture
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Something wedged in a cupboard might be off a broken necklace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests an object, but it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: A necklace is made of small pierced balls threaded on a string, each one a bead.

clue.text: Pleasurable things given sign of approval — an element in computer game?

parts.note: joys are delights
a tick mark shows something is correct

explanation.surface: Fun things get a thumbs-up as part of a video game.
explanation.walkthrough: A tick is the British check mark used to show approval.
explanation.definitionFit: A joystick is the hand-held lever controller used to play video games.

clue.text: Auntie, I'm fussed about minor details

indicators.note: being in a fuss means flustered and disordered

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A niece or nephew confesses to fretting over trifles.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in the contraction is ignored; the eight letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Minutiae are the small, precise or trivial particulars of something, a Latin plural meaning trifles.

clue.text: Roving in bad van, go mad

indicators.note: something gone crazy is out of its proper order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Travelling about in a clapped-out van drives you crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: Vagabond is used here as an adjective, wandering.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it describes a wandering, homeless life, travelling from place to place.

clue.text: God of old, big noise

parts.note: standard abbreviation for old
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: An ancient deity, a great clamour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God of old' reads as one phrase, but the definition ends at the first word. 'Big noise' could mean an important person; it is a racket.
explanation.definitionFit: Odin is the chief of the Norse gods, ruler of Asgard.

clue.text: Knave with bundle returning, a proverbial thief

parts.note: the knave is the jack in a pack of cards

indicators.note: coming back means travelling the other way along the line

parts.note: a wad is a bundle, as of banknotes

explanation.surface: A rogue comes back with a bundle of loot, like a famous thief.
explanation.walkthrough: Knave and jack are the same playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackdaw, a small crow, is reputed in folklore to steal shiny objects.

clue.text: Eminence not right — stony-looking character?

indicators.note: without a thing means it is taken away

parts.note: stature is standing or eminence
standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A grand figure who is wrong and stony-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R from the word for eminence, leaving STATUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a carved figure, typically in stone, so literally a character that looks stony.

clue.text: Mechanical device — power is coming with great speed

parts.note: P is the symbol for power
taken as written
a ton is a hundred miles an hour

explanation.surface: A machine part delivering power at high speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A ton' is British slang for a hundred miles per hour, a speed bikers boast of.
explanation.definitionFit: A piston is the sliding cylinder in an engine that converts pressure into motion.

clue.text: Money given to the German who supplies grub?

definitions.note: a relative clause; the answer is the noun for the one who does it

parts.note: a fee is money paid
der is the German masculine definite article

explanation.surface: Payment handed to the German caterer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The German' is a crossword convention for a German article such as DER, DIE or DAS.
explanation.definitionFit: A feeder is something or someone providing food, such as a bird feeder supplying seed.

clue.text: One who can't stand being in another's house?

definitions.text: One who can't stand being in another's house?

parts.words: One who can't stand being in another's house?
parts.note: surface reading: someone who hates staying at other people's homes
setter's reading: one who crouches rather than stands, and who occupies a house without right

explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't stand' means dislike on the surface, but literally means sitting low on the heels.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who unlawfully occupies an empty building; the word also names a person crouching.

clue.text: Dog's getting about square after four

definitions.note: a possessive in the clue; the answer is the adjective meaning of dogs

parts.note: ca is circa, Latin for about
the next square number after four is three times three

explanation.surface: A dog gets round a town square just after four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square after four' sounds like a time and place, but means the next perfect square in the sequence 1, 4, 9.
explanation.definitionFit: Canine means relating to dogs, so it stands for the possessive form.

clue.text: Foreign character stuck in maze tantalisingly

indicators.note: lodged inside the following words, spanning their letters

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An alien figure trapped teasingly in a labyrinth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foreign character' sounds like a stranger, but it is a letter of a foreign alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeta is the sixth letter of the Greek alphabet, a character from a foreign script.

clue.text: Fools one spots traversing island

parts.note: Roman numeral one

indicators.note: to traverse is to lie across, so one part spans around another

parts.note: spots are dots
standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A fool sees people crossing an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' looks like a verb, sees, but it is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiot is a fool, a stupid person; both are plural nouns here.

clue.text: Left in grass, covered in newspaper?

indicators.note: the word places one part within another

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: Something abandoned in the grass, wrapped up in newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Covered in newspaper' suggests wrapping; it means written up by the press. 'Left' is nautical port.
explanation.definitionFit: A story that journalists have covered has been written up as news in the papers.

clue.text: Presumably one who has found football player?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: from the saying 'finders ..., losers weepers'

explanation.walkthrough: The first half relies on the children's rhyme claiming that whoever finds something may keep it; 'presumably' admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalie is short-named this in football, and the playground saying gives finders the right to retain things.

clue.text: Medieval cleric finished being embraced by one of Henry's wives

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around, so one part holds another inside

parts.note: Catherine Parr was Henry VIII's sixth wife
done means finished

explanation.surface: A churchman done for in the arms of one of Henry VIII's queens.
explanation.walkthrough: Of Henry VIII's six wives, only Parr has a surname that fits around the middle piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A pardoner was a medieval churchman licensed to sell indulgences, as in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.
